# Distributed ML Principles {.unnumbered}

Coordinating the fleet requires solving problems that a single machine does not. If Part I built the physical substrate, Part II establishes the logic of distribution: the algorithms, protocols, and coordination strategies that transform a collection of independent accelerators into a singular, unified machine. The physics of distributed learning governs this transition, supplying the first-principles reasoning that explains why adding more GPUs does not always yield linear speedups, and why communication, not computation, is often the hidden bottleneck.

At this scale, the engineering challenge is a trade-off between parallelization and coordination. Partitioning a model reduces per-device memory pressure but requires exchanging intermediate results across partitions. Replicating a model across workers instead requires coordinating their updates. Adding nodes can reduce training time while exposing a job to more component failures, decreasing its mean time between failures (MTBF) when an individual failure interrupts the job. Fault tolerance therefore becomes part of the execution design. These principles decompose the communication tax introduced in Part I and add the reliability tax of scale.

The following principles preview the trade-offs developed in Part II. A checkpoint is a saved training state from which execution can resume after failure; communication overlap means executing useful computation while data transfers proceed. The chapters establish when these mechanisms help and how to measure their costs. The first pressure is the economics of scale itself: frontier capability demands compute, but each improvement gets progressively more expensive.

```{=latex}
\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}
```

::: {#pri-universal-scaling .callout-principle title="The universal scaling law"}

**Invariant**: Within empirically validated regimes, foundation-model loss ($\mathcal{L}$) follows approximate power-law relationships with compute ($C$), dataset size ($D$), and parameters ($P$). The exponent $\gamma$ depends on the fitted regime. The compute-only simplification used to illustrate diminishing returns is:
$$ \mathcal{L}(C) \propto C^{-\gamma} $$

**Implication**: Within a fixed scaling regime, reducing loss further requires increasing resources. The diminishing return helps explain the move from single-server training to warehouse-scale clusters. Architecture, data quality, and training methods can change that regime, so a fitted scaling relation guides resource planning without guaranteeing improvements on every task.

:::

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}
```

That demand for scale turns each training step into a negotiation between faster local work and slower global coordination.

::: {#pri-distributed-step-time .callout-principle title="The fleet law (distributed step time law)"}

**Invariant**: Under ideal partitioning of a fixed amount of work across $N$ workers or accelerators, the step-time model adds computation, communication, and synchronization, then subtracts the portion hidden by overlap, with $0 \le T_{\text{overlap}} \le \min\!\left(\frac{T_{\text{compute}}}{N}, T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N)\right)$.
$$ T_{\text{step}}(N) = \frac{T_{\text{compute}}}{N} + T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}} $$

**Implication**: Scaling is a race between parallelizable compute (which shrinks with $N$ under ideal partitioning), communication overhead, and synchronization overhead. To scale efficiently, algorithms must reduce or amortize $T_{\text{comm}}(N)$ and $T_{\text{sync}}(N)$ (for example, through gradient accumulation, which alters the effective batch and convergence regime, or through compression, which can introduce numerical error) and maximize $T_{\text{overlap}}$ through communication hiding and pipelined execution.

:::

The communication term in that negotiation is governed by the interconnect's latency and bandwidth, so message size determines which optimization helps.

::: {#pri-alpha-beta-model .callout-principle title="The bandwidth-latency trade-off (α-β model)"}

**Invariant**: In the latency-bandwidth model, communication time combines fixed startup latency ($\alpha$) with the transfer time for a message of size $n$ at effective bandwidth $\beta$.
$$ T(n) = \alpha + \frac{n}{\beta} $$

**Implication**: Small messages (for example, mixture-of-experts routing metadata) are latency-bound; large messages (for example, gradients) are bandwidth-bound. Optimization strategies must match the regime: fuse small messages to amortize $\alpha$, compress large messages to reduce $n$.

:::

Even when communication is tuned, a larger fleet fails often enough that progress itself must be protected.

::: {#pri-young-daly .callout-principle title="The Young-Daly checkpoint law"}

**Invariant**: The first-order checkpoint model balances the cost of writing the checkpoint ($T_{\text{write}}$) against the expected cost of reworking lost progress due to system-level failures ($\text{MTBF}_{\text{system}}$). For long runs with approximately constant failure rates and checkpoint write times small relative to MTBF, its optimal interval ($\tau_{\text{opt}}$) is:
$$ \tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot T_{\text{write}} \cdot \text{MTBF}_{\text{system}}} $$

**Implication**: Checkpointing consumes time and storage bandwidth. When more participating components reduce job MTBF, the model favors shorter intervals; faster checkpoint writes can reduce that overhead. Correlated failures, variable write times, and recovery requirements need additional analysis before the interval becomes an operational schedule.

:::

Fault tolerance illustrates why reducing one cost requires checking the others: saving more often reduces expected rework but increases storage traffic.

::: {#pri-conservation-overhead .callout-principle title="The displacement of overhead"}

**Invariant**: Distributed ML optimizations often relocate overhead among Compute, Communication, and Coordination (the C$^3$ taxonomy). Reducing one term can increase another, so designs must evaluate all three.

**Implication**: Asynchronous training can eliminate global coordination barriers ($T_{\text{sync}}(N) \to 0$) but may introduce gradient staleness that manifests as additional training iterations ($T_{\text{compute}} \uparrow$). Pipeline parallelism can reduce communication volume relative to finer-grained model partitioning but adds pipeline bubble time ($T_{\text{sync}}(N) \uparrow$). The C$^3$ taxonomy reveals where each design pays its overhead.

:::

Part II develops these previews in dependency order. Distributed training establishes how to partition a workload and what information the partitions must exchange. Collective communication then explains how groups of workers combine and redistribute that information efficiently. Fault tolerance protects the resulting progress against failure, and fleet orchestration allocates shared resources to jobs with those communication and recovery needs. Together, these chapters develop the algorithmic and operational discipline that turns the physical fleet of Part I into a working distributed training system.
